lesson.child_mission: Data are raw facts or signals (numbers, clicks, sensor readings). Information is data given context and meaning so a person can use it. The same number can be useless alone and useful once labelled.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same technology/design idea to a new object or material, then compare two pieces of evidence for strength.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Sort: “72”, “heart rate 72 bpm after walking”, “blue”. Which are data only, and which are information?

FEEDBACK
“72” and “blue” are bare data. “Heart rate 72 bpm after walking” is information with context.

WATCH FOR
Calling any spreadsheet “information” even when columns are unlabelled. Without context it stays raw data.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Write one data-only example and rewrite it as information by adding unit, time, or place. School-safe examples only.

Write a short reflection naming one observation, criterion or step you corrected and why.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
The digits 16 alone are data. “16 °C on the classroom thermometer at 9 am” is information because unit, place, and time give meaning.

TRY FIRST
Sort: “72”, “heart rate 72 bpm after walking”, “blue”. Which are data only, and which are information?

FEEDBACK
“72” and “blue” are bare data. “Heart rate 72 bpm after walking” is information with context.
teach_steps.explain:
Data are raw facts or signals (numbers, clicks, sensor readings). Information is data given context and meaning so a person can use it. The same number can be useless alone and useful once labelled.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen, measured or tested against criteria.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the observations, properties, criteria or test steps that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your record with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your evidence? If a result is uncertain, identify what would have to be observed or tested again. One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer. For practical technology work, follow teacher safety rules for tools, food and devices.
